author: Al Jazeera English
description:
The Iran war has severely disrupted oil and gas flows through the Strait of Hormuz, a route normally used for around 20% of the world’s oil and gas supplies.

That has cut off oil and gas supplies from the Gulf to Asia and Europe.

Pressure has also spread to Bab al-Mandeb in the Red Sea, while Ukrainian attacks on Russian infrastructure has affected exports through the Black Sea.

Diplomatic efforts continue to reach a final deal, but the situation remains volatile and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz are yet to be fully restored.

Oil prices respond not only to barrels already removed from the market, but also to expectations of what could happen next.

Goldman Sachs has warned that Brent could rise above $120 a barrel, if disruption through the Strait of Hormuz persists.

Higher energy prices spread through the wider economy, increasing the cost of almost everything from transport to manufacturing, air travel to food.

Consumers across the world are starting to feel the pinch
title: Oil prices: Worth It? | Counting the Cost

Iran is advancing regional diplomacy while maintaining strategic leverage over the Strait of Hormuz. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said talks with Oman on a maritime framework for the waterway are in their final stages, while Tehran continues consultations with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan on regional security and stability. However, Iranian officials stressed that the talks with Oman are bilateral and not part of negotiations with the United States, warning they do not guarantee the Strait of Hormuz will reopen. Tehran says the waterway will not return to pre-war conditions, accusing Washington of carrying out attacks against Iran before an agreed timeline expired. The developments reflect Iran's dual-track strategy of expanding diplomatic outreach while maintaining deterrence and keeping the Strait of Hormuz as a key source of strategic leverage.

Al Jazeera's Mahmoud Abdelwahed reports from Tehran.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
In an interview with Al Jazeera, former US Ambassador to Bahrain Adam Ereli cast doubt on President Donald Trump's claim that a deal with Iran is imminent on the Strait of Hormuz and denuclearisation. Ereli said: "I don't see Iran, unless Trump makes some significant concessions, I don't see them changing their position." He argued that Iran is holding the world "hostage" and that "time, frankly, is on their side." Ereli suggested the US should return to the tough sanctions regime of the Obama era, which pressured Iran into the 2015 nuclear deal, but noted that Trump is unlikely to adopt that approach and has alienated international partners. Ereli predicted Trump will "muddle through" with a combination of "bluster, cajoling and persuasion" to get something he can call a victory, comparing it to Trump's recent Gaza announcement which he described as "hooey." He also said public opinion is unlikely to influence Trump's decisions as he is a lame-duck president.
